# Dataset background and description

a) brief summary of data set

```{r}
# This data set was created by Glassdoor Economic Research to help HR practitioners perform their own internal gender pay audit. This data set has sample gender pay gap data for a hypothetical employer with 1,000 employees across 10 job roles and 5 company departments. 
```

b) motivation for choosing the data set

```{r}
# As a rising 4th year, I am envisioning what my life will soon like when I enter the industry. Part of that involves thinking and comparing salaries and job positions.

# However, as a woman who wants to enter the tech industry, a primarily male-dominated field, I know that I may not be as equally valued to male co-workers. 

# For years, I've been working (first an intern, now part-time employee) at a tech company in their HR and AP department. I know that the gender pay gap is still a real and pressing issue on a social, legal, and business standpoint. 

# I chose this data set because I wanted to learn more about how I can analyze the gender pay gap myself and was curious about what results this analysis would produce.
```

# Data preparation and summary: manipulation and summary of relevant variables

a) data cleaning

```{r}
# load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(stargazer)
library(ggplot2)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(caret)
library(ISLR)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(car)

```


```{r}
# load data set and save to data frame
GPG<-read.csv("Glassdoor Gender Pay Gap.csv")

# add above and below median base pay variable
# add total pay for year (base + bonus)
gpg<-GPG%>%
  mutate("TotalPay"=BasePay+Bonus)%>%
  mutate("BelowMedianPay"=ifelse(TotalPay<100047, "Yes", "No"))

# find median of total pay of entire company
summary(gpg$TotalPay) 

# create factor for education to order education levels
gpg$Education<-factor(gpg$Education, levels=c("High School", "College", "Masters", "PhD"))

```

b) sub-setting to summarize key variables

```{r}
# only females
females<-gpg%>%
  filter(Gender=="Female")

# only males
males<-gpg%>%
  filter(Gender=="Male")

# job titles
jobs<-gpg%>%
  select(JobTitle)%>%
  table()
jobs

# departments
depts<-gpg%>%
  select(Dept)%>%
  table()
depts

# filter age groups (under 30, 30-50, 50+)
young<-gpg%>%
  filter(Age<30)
  
mid<-gpg%>%
  filter(Age>=30 & Age<50)
  
old<-gpg%>%
  filter(Age>50)

# filter by education
hs<-gpg%>%
  filter(Education=="High School")

college<-gpg%>%
  filter(Education=="College")

masters<-gpg%>%
  filter(Education=="Masters")

phd<-gpg%>%
  filter(Education=="PhD")

# filter by level of seniority
entrylevel<-gpg%>%
  filter(Seniority<3)

seniorlevel<-gpg%>%
  filter(Seniority>=3)

```

c) Summary measures

```{r}
glimpse(gpg)

# summaries of numeric variables: Age, PerfEval, Seniority, BasePay, Bonus

summary(gpg$Age)
summary(gpg$PerfEval)
summary(gpg$Seniority)
summary(gpg$BasePay)
summary(gpg$Bonus)
summary(gpg$TotalPay)

# numerical summaries by gender
tapply(gpg$Age, gpg$Gender, summary)
tapply(gpg$PerfEval, gpg$Gender, summary)
tapply(gpg$Seniority, gpg$Gender, summary)
tapply(gpg$BasePay, gpg$Gender, summary)
tapply(gpg$Bonus, gpg$Gender, summary)
tapply(gpg$TotalPay, gpg$Gender, summary)

# data frame summary of overall male-female pay differences in base pay
gpg_summary<-gpg%>%
  group_by(Gender)%>%
  summarise("Mean Base Pay"=mean(BasePay, na.rm=TRUE), "Median Base Pay"=median(BasePay, na.rm=TRUE), "Observations"=sum(!(is.na(BasePay))))

View(gpg_summary)

# summaries of categorical variables: JobTitle, Gender, Education, Dept
# frequency tables
table(gpg$JobTitle)
table(gpg$Gender)
table(gpg$Education)
table(gpg$Dept)
table(gpg$BelowMedianPay)

# 2-way tables
table(gpg$JobTitle, gpg$Gender)
table(gpg$Dept, gpg$Gender)
table(gpg$Education, gpg$Gender)

# spread of employees across job titles
job_summary<-gpg%>%
  group_by(JobTitle, Gender)%>%
  summarise("Mean Total Pay"=mean(TotalPay, na.rm=TRUE), Employees=sum(!(is.na(JobTitle))))

View(job_summary)

```

# Data visualization

a)

```{r}
# bar graph of key categorical variables

# 2 categorical variables: stacked/percent-stacked/side-by-side dodge bar graph
# How many employees take up each position in the company, and how many are male and female?
ggplot(gpg,aes(x=JobTitle,fill=Gender))+geom_bar(position="dodge")+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=90))+labs(x="Job Titles", y="Number of Employees", title="Gender of Employee Positions")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

# histogram/boxplot of key numerical variables
ggplot(gpg, aes(y=TotalPay))+geom_boxplot(fill="darkseagreen4")+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=90))+labs(y="Total Pay (USD)", title="Total Pay Summary")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

```


b)

```{r}

ggplot(gpg, aes(x=Gender, y=TotalPay, fill=Gender))+geom_boxplot()+labs(x="Gender", y="Total Pay (USD)", title="Total Pay Difference Female vs. Male")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

# Regression

a)

```{r}
# multiple or simple linear regression

glimpse(gpg)
# select desired variables to a new data frame
nd<-select(gpg, Age, PerfEval, Seniority, TotalPay)

# build correlation matrix to calc correlation amongst selected variables
cor_matrix<-round(cor(nd),2)
View(cor_matrix)

# plot correlations in correlogram
ggcorrplot(cor_matrix, type="lower", lab=T)

# build multilinear model
pay_model<-train(TotalPay~., nd, method="lm")
summary(pay_model)

# get final model
pay_model$finalModel

# VIF
vif(pay_model$finalModel)

# AIC
better_model<-train(TotalPay~., nd, method="lmStepAIC", trace=F)
summary(better_model)

# Interpretation
# Holding all other variables fixed, for every 1 increment increase in level of  Seniority, the TotalPay increases by $9,796.53.

# About 58.17% of the variability in TotalPay can be explained by this multiple regression model.

# The predictive power of this model is 58.04%

# pick reasonable values for predictor variables to make a prediction of the response variable

# create new data point
new<-data.frame(Age=22, PerfEval=3, Seniority=1)

# make a prediction using new data point and best model
predict(better_model, new)

# given the data provided for age, perfeval, and seniority, the model predicts that the employee will be paid a total of $62,871.48.

# equation: TotalPay = 28823.78 + 965.41*Age + 1004.04*PerfEval + 9796.53*Seniority

```

b)

```{r}
# logistic regression model 
# is being a female related to total pay (being above/below median pay)?
# how to tell if 2 categorical variables are related/independent:
ggplot(gpg, aes(x=Gender, fill=BelowMedianPay))+geom_bar(position = "fill")

# extract only females, select desired variables for new data frame 
amp<-gpg%>%
  filter(Gender=="Female")%>%
  select(BelowMedianPay, Age, PerfEval, Seniority)
View(amp)

# extract only predictor variables (BelowMedianPay is used as response variable)
VAR<-select(amp,-BelowMedianPay)
View(VAR)

# calc correlation matrix
cor_mat2<-round(cor(VAR),2)
View(cor_mat2)
ggcorrplot(cor_mat2, type="lower", lab=TRUE)

# create logit model
logit<-train(BelowMedianPay~., amp, method="glm", family="binomial")
summary(logit)

# VIF
vif(logit$finalModel)

# use best predictors w/ StepAIC
logit_aic<-train(BelowMedianPay~., amp, method="glmStepAIC",family="binomial",direction="both", trace=FALSE)
summary(logit_aic)

# exponentiation
exp(coef(logit_aic$finalModel))

# Failure = 0 = No
# Success = 1 = Yes
# Interpret change of odds of being above median

# age odds calc
(1-0.8849649)*100

# Odds interpretation for age
# Holding all other variables in the model fixed, for every year increase in age among female employees, the odds of having a total pay below median decreases by 12%.

# perfeval odds calc
(1-0.8722995)*100

# odds interpretation for perfeval
# Holding all other variables in the model fixed, for each increment increase in perfeval among female employees, the odds of having a total pay below median decreases by 13%.


# seniority odds calc
(1-0.2818193)*100

# odds interpretation for seniority
# Holding all other variables in the model fixed, for each increasing level in seniority among female employees, the odds of having a total pay below median decreases by 72%


# pick reasonable values for predictor variables to make a prediction of the response variable

new2<-data.frame(Age=22, PerfEval=3, Seniority=1)
predict(logit_aic,new2)

# equation:
# ln(p/(1-p)) = 9.80726 -0.12221*Age - 0.13662*PerfEval - 1.26649*Seniority
```


# Classification

```{r}
# KNN model

# make graphs to find closest neighbor
ggplot(gpg, aes(x=Seniority, y=TotalPay, color=Gender))+geom_point()+labs(x="Seniority", y="Total Pay (USD)", title="Seniority vs. Total Pay")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

# make a point
new_emp<-data.frame(Seniority=4, TotalPay=100000)

# add new point to graph, specifying color
ggplot(gpg, aes(x=Seniority, y=TotalPay, color=Gender))+geom_point()+geom_point(data=new_emp,color="black")+labs(x="Seniority", y="Total Pay (USD)", title="Seniority vs. Total Pay")+theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

# build model
knn_model<-train(Gender~Seniority+TotalPay,gpg,method="knn")

# find how mnay nearest neighbors to count
knn_model$finalModel

# find out why they chose optimal number of neighbors to pick
ggplot(knn_model)

# pick reasonable values for predictor variables to make a prediction of the response variable

predict(knn_model,new_emp)
```
